representations.text: During March 30–April 12, a four-day change on April 3–6 interrupted otherwise stable readings: resting heart rate rose to 65–67 bpm versus the 28-day baseline mean of 56.0, while RMSSD fell to 23–26 ms versus 45. Both returned to baseline ranges on April 7 and remained there through April 12. Window means were 58.7 bpm and 38.9 ms; their strong inverse association (r=-0.97) reflects this coincident episode, which crossed weekdays and the first weekend. Sleep and movement showed no corresponding shift: sleep averaged 470 versus 470 minutes, steps 7,996 versus 8,043, active minutes 55.3 versus 54.9, and low movement 447 versus 451 minutes. Sleep starts stayed near 22:50 with 07:00 waking and little weekday/weekend difference. Activity remained one 21:00 bout; daytime low movement comprised ten roughly 44–46-minute bouts separated by five-minute gaps. Activity duration had little association with sleep ending the following day (r=0.10). All metrics were complete.

Sleep changed abruptly from a stable 28-day baseline of 469 minutes, approximately 22:51–07:00, to a repeating weekday/weekend pattern throughout March 30–April 12. All ten weekday sleeps lasted 386–393 minutes (mean 390, down 79), starting 00:07–00:14 with waking still at 07:00. Both weekends had 565–575 minutes (mean 570, up 101), starting 01:05–01:15 and ending at 11:00. After the first weekend, short weekday sleep resumed April 6; baseline timing never returned. The overall mean of 441 minutes obscures this alternation, and the positive overall slope does not represent sustained lengthening. Other means stayed close to baseline: steps 7,939 versus 8,019, active minutes 54.7 versus 55.4, low movement 451 versus 451, resting heart rate 56.1 versus 56.5 bpm, and RMSSD 45.4 versus 45.3 ms. Activity stayed at 21:00; interrupted low-movement bouts began at 11:30 on weekends versus 10:00 weekdays. Activity duration weakly related to following-day sleep (r=-0.15). All metrics were complete.

Steps rose abruptly on March 30 and stayed elevated for all 14 days through April 12: mean 7,927 versus the 28-day baseline of 2,818, an increase of 5,109/day (181%). Every window day (7,636–8,320) exceeded the baseline range (2,565–3,023), with no return despite a slight downward window trend. Weekend steps averaged 8,126 versus 7,847 on weekdays; baseline groups both averaged about 2,818. This increase was not accompanied by more active minutes: 55.3 versus 56.2 overall, with weekends falling to 52.5 from 57.3 while weekdays averaged 56.4 versus 55.8. Activity remained a single 21:00 bout. Low movement changed little, averaging 447 versus 451 minutes across ten daytime bouts separated by five-minute gaps. Sleep remained near baseline (469 versus 471 minutes), with starts near 22:50, fixed 07:00 waking, and little weekday/weekend difference. Resting heart rate remained 55–57 bpm and RMSSD 43–47 ms. Activity duration had little association with following-day sleep (r=-0.10), and steps weakly related to active minutes (r=-0.10). All metrics were complete.

Steps dropped abruptly on March 30 and remained below baseline throughout all 14 days through April 12: mean 2,335 versus the preceding 28-day mean of 8,009, down 5,675/day (71%). Every window day (2,064–2,636) was below the baseline range (7,607–8,342), with no recovery. Weekends averaged 2,477 steps versus 2,278 on weekdays, but both remained markedly reduced. Active minutes stayed near baseline overall (54.6 versus 55.1); weekends declined to 52.3 from 56.9, while weekdays averaged 55.5 versus 54.5. Activity remained one 21:00 bout, and low movement stayed near 453 versus 451 minutes across ten daytime bouts interrupted by five-minute gaps. Sleep remained stable at 470 minutes, with starts near 22:50 and fixed 07:00 waking. Resting heart rate averaged 56.0 versus 55.7 bpm; RMSSD averaged 45.3 versus 45.1 ms, declining slightly within its baseline range. Window associations were moderately inverse for heart rate/RMSSD (r=-0.57) and weaker for activity/following-day sleep (r=-0.36); neither establishes causation. All metrics were complete.
